title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
trick: Buy training data at a mix of solver accuracies, tag each sample with its accuracy, and tune the mix: at a fixed simulation budget, many cheap-and-wrong samples plus a few accurate ones beat accurate-only.
framing_stripped: Called compute-optimal multi-fidelity data scaling with Pareto-optimal error frontiers; it is a one-parameter sampling distribution over solver settings (coarser mesh or fewer iterations) plus a scalar conditioning input that tells the network how wrong each label is, swept by brute force for the best setting at each budget.
method: Simulator P_h(f_h; xi) maps an input field f_h to a solution u_h at fidelity xi (larger xi = more accurate). Error of the simulator at fidelity xi: e(xi) = E_f[ ||P_h(f; xi) - P_h(f; inf)||_2 / ||P_h(f; inf)||_2 ]. Two error sources with known decay: discretization, xi = resolution N (grid points or mesh nodes), e(N) = O(N^-alpha) with alpha > 0 (Poisson: second order in points per dimension; P1 finite elements on the von Mises stress: empirical alpha = 0.68 linear elasticity, 0.70 hyperelasticity; airfoil fields: alpha = 1.04); iterative-solver truncation, xi = iteration count K, e(K) = O(rho^K) with contraction factor rho in (0,1) (symmetric Gauss-Seidel on elasticity: rho ~ 0.99994; chord Newton on hyperelasticity: rho ~ 0.95; multigrid V-cycles on Poisson: rho from Fig. 12). Cost per sample c(xi): c(K) = K iterations (mesh fixed, so per-iteration cost factors out); c(N) = N^D grid points for the D-dimensional Poisson direct solve, c(N) = N mesh nodes for the finite-element LU solve, and measured CPU core-hours for the airfoil (0.9 to 8.3 core-hours per sample). Budget B; normalized budget B_tilde = B / c(xi_max) = the number of top-fidelity samples B would buy. Fidelity menu Xi = {xi_1, ..., xi_|Xi|} anchored so that e(xi_min) is in [10%, 30%] (about 20%) and e(xi_max) is about 0.5% (slightly below the surrogate's own error floor). Normalized fidelity, linear in the theoretical error: xi_hat(xi) = (e(xi_min) - e(xi)) / (e(xi_min) - e(xi_max)) in [0,1], computed from the convergence law, not from a per-sample reference solve. Mixture: p(xi_hat_i; lambda, Xi) = exp(lambda xi_hat_i) / sum_j exp(lambda xi_hat_j); lambda > 0 favors accurate samples, lambda < 0 cheap ones, lambda = 0 uniform; lambda = +20 in practice is the high-fidelity-only baseline. Budgeted sampler: draw fidelities i.i.d. from p until sum_j c(xi^(j)) >= B, giving M samples with E[M] ~ B / E_p[c(xi)]; each sample's label is generated at its own fidelity. Surrogate S_theta(f_h; xi_hat) is trained by empirical risk minimization on all (f_h, u_h, xi) triples with loss zeta (per-pixel MSE on grids; field-averaged relative L2 on meshes). Test error E(lambda, B) = relative L2 of S_theta(f; xi_hat(xi_max)) against P_h(f; xi_max) on held-out top-fidelity data, so the residual e(xi_max) is absorbed into the definition of truth. Compute-optimal mixture: lambda*(B) = argmin_lambda E(lambda, B), found by sweeping a grid of lambda values (7 to ~20 mixtures) at each budget; the frontier is B -> E(lambda*(B), B). Claims verified: C1, for B below a problem-dependent crossover B_max the optimum is interior (lambda* finite, E(lambda*, B) < E(+inf, B)); C2, lambda* -> +inf and the two curves merge as B -> inf. Savings S(E*) = ratio of high-fidelity-only budget to multi-fidelity budget at a target error E* (10% for Poisson and elasticity, 2% for airfoil volume fields): mean ~3.1x over 20 setups, max 6.3x (linear elasticity, solver axis). Post-hoc calibration recipe for lambda* without the sweep: lambda*(B_tilde) = a + b log(B_tilde), fit on 7 mixtures at 3 small budgets; held-out regret r = E(lambda_pred)/E(lambda*) - 1 is < 5% on solver axes, <= 10% on mesh discretization axes, and 49% to 99% on Poisson discretization axes where lambda* jumps abruptly; calibration overhead ~51% of the deployment budget at 2x the calibration ceiling, ~9% at 16x, versus +170% for sweeping lambda directly at the deployment budget.
setup: Six PDE problems, two error axes each except airfoil, four architectures, over 7,000 training runs and over 12,000 GPU-hours; all steady-state. (1-3) Poisson equation in 1D, 2D, 3D on a 64^D finite-difference grid: discretization axis = native resolution N (menus {20,28,36,48}, {20,32,48,64,96}, {16,24,32,48,64,96}; solved exactly by discrete sine transform, then input and output interpolated to 64^D, so low-fidelity samples carry discretization plus interpolation error); solver axis = K geometric-multigrid V-cycles from a zero guess (red-black Gauss-Seidel smoother, 2 pre/post sweeps, 50 coarsest sweeps, 5 levels; menus {1,2,3}, {1..7}, {2..8}); B_tilde 10 to 10^4; FiLM-conditioned U-Net (10.9M params main; 0.69M to 43.65M in ablation) and FNO; 20,000 Adam steps. (4) Linear elasticity, 2D perforated steel plate (5-20 holes, random traction), P1 triangular finite elements in FEniCSx/PETSc, target = von Mises stress: discretization axis = mesh nodes 212 to 29,408 (21 levels, direct LU/MUMPS, B_tilde 100-3,200); solver axis = symmetric Gauss-Seidel (SSOR Richardson, omega = 1) iterations 25,000 to 262,144 (11 levels, mesh fixed, B_tilde 100-6,400). (5) Hyperelasticity, same geometry with a compressible Neo-Hookean elastomer (E = 2 MPa, strains to 30%): discretization axis identical menu (full Newton-Raphson to 1e-6 so solver error is negligible); solver axis = chord Newton with Jacobian frozen at the zero guess, 20 to 190 iterations (16 levels, mesh fixed at ~1,600 nodes). Architectures for (4)-(5): Transolver and AB-UPT. (6) Airfoil external aerodynamics, steady incompressible RANS with k-omega SST in OpenFOAM simpleFoam (SIMPLEC, 20k or 40k outer iterations fixed), NACA 4/5-digit shapes, Re 2e6-6e6, AoA -5 to 15 deg: discretization axis only, 11 mesh levels from ~7,600 to ~180,000 nodes costing 0.9 to 8.3 CPU core-hours each (all top-fidelity samples: 13,580 core-hours on a 96-core EPYC); B_tilde 50-800; Transolver and AB-UPT; no solver axis because SIMPLEC convergence is non-monotone in the outer-iteration count and depends on several interacting tolerances. Spectrum-vs-binary ablation: 19 intermediate resolutions give 33% lower error than coarsest+finest only on hyperelasticity discretization; on the narrower solver axis the binary mixture is marginally better at its optimum.
load_bearing_assumption: The simulator's error at a given setting is a systematic, monotone function of that setting alone, predictable from the convergence law for every sample, so a scalar tag lets the network separate the input-to-output map from the fidelity-induced bias; the paper itself declines the SIMPLEC axis because its convergence is non-monotone and multi-knob, and assumes data generation cost dominates training cost and the model is large enough to absorb the extra samples.
weakest_component: The optimal mixture lambda* is an oracle obtained by sweeping 7 to ~20 mixtures at every budget; the headline 6.3x saving excludes that search (+170% at the deployment budget, or +51% via the calibration recipe, which fails with 49% to 99% regret on the Poisson discretization axis when the optimum jumps). Second: truth is the top of the menu, not a converged solution, and xi_max is placed at e ~ 0.5%, below the surrogate's own floor, so the saving is measured against a label the network cannot beat anyway; the converged-reference check (L.7) was run only on the 2D Poisson solver axis, where it moved results by at most 0.5%; the mesh experiments could not be converged. Third: on the Poisson grids the discretization axis is partly multilinear interpolation error (L.3), not pure solver resolution.
regime: Steady-state PDEs only (no time stepping, no rollout horizon): Poisson 1D/2D/3D on 64^D grids, 2D linear and Neo-Hookean elasticity on unstructured meshes, 2D RANS airfoils. Surrogates: FiLM U-Net 0.69M-43.65M params and FNO on grids; Transolver and AB-UPT on meshes. Error band: simulator menus span 10-30% (coarsest) to 0.4-1% (finest) relative L2; surrogates land at 1.4-20% depending on budget. Budgets: 10 to 10^4 high-fidelity-equivalent samples (Poisson), 100-6,400 (elasticity), 50-800 (airfoil, where one top sample costs 8.3 CPU core-hours). Largest gains at 100-500 high-fidelity-equivalent samples; curves merge at large budgets. Compute: >7,000 runs, >12,000 GPU-hours; each run 20,000 update steps regardless of dataset size.
information_asymmetry: Stage where the method runs: data generation and surrogate training for a PDE with a known convergence law. Information the paper has there and uses: the per-sample error e(xi) as a closed-form function of the solver setting (second-order in N; geometric in K with a fixed contraction factor rho), which gives the normalized tag xi_hat without ever computing the fine reference for that sample; a constant cost c(xi) per setting; and a clean single knob. Stage where this information is missing: RL training in a GPU-batched rigid-body engine with contact. There the per-step fidelity is set by an iteration cap on a Newton or projected Gauss-Seidel contact solver and a time step, but (a) no convergence law is known for the capped contact solve (non-smooth complementarity, warm starts, per-world residuals that differ by orders of magnitude; the paper's own reason for refusing the SIMPLEC axis applies: convergence non-monotone in the outer count and governed by several interacting tolerances), so xi_hat cannot be written down and the paper's whole normalization (Eq. 14) is unavailable; (b) the information that would replace the law does exist inside the engine at step time, the achieved residual and the fact that the cap was hit per world per step, and is discarded before the policy sees the state, so fidelity is unobserved by the consumer instead of a conditioning input; (c) the policy is not a regressor toward the top-fidelity label but an optimizer of return inside the low-fidelity dynamics, and the paper never measures whether a consumer that optimizes, rather than regresses, exploits the low-fidelity error (the surrogate is always tested at xi_hat(xi_max) against xi_max labels, with fidelities drawn i.i.d. per sample and no compounding across steps); (d) the paper excludes modeling error and reality, so e(xi) is distance to a finer solve, never to a measured impact. What exists in hindsight that the paper never uses at generation time: the surrogate's eventual error floor, which fixes where xi_max should sit; they set it by a 0.5% rule of thumb and a sweep.
occupies: Fidelity as a fine-grained menu with a one-parameter softmax mixture over it, a fidelity-conditioned surrogate, the test-error-versus-data-generation-compute Pareto frontier across both the discretization and the iterative-solver axis (claimed first for the solver axis), the recommendation that the solver-iteration axis is the practical one, the 0.5%/20% endpoint-anchoring rule, and the log-linear lambda*(B) calibration recipe.

neighbors.trick: unknown (not fetched); 2610.17221 states it exploits the same solver-iteration truncation axis at training time inside differentiable-physics training loops.

theme_fit.why: Fidelity as a tunable dose with a known convergence rate, and the two knobs it turns (spatial resolution, iterative-solver truncation) are exactly the time step and iteration cap that GPU physics engines set silently; but the consumer is a regressor tested against the top-fidelity label, never a policy that optimizes inside the coarse dynamics, and the paper refuses any axis whose convergence is non-monotone, which is the contact-solver case.
Treats data generation, not training, as the dominant cost and builds a compute-matched error-versus-generation-cost frontier; no agent or RL workload attached.

limitations_as_complaints: My problems are transient, not steady-state: the paper covers only steady problems and says that for rollouts the time step would have to become a fidelity axis, which needs an architecture that handles varying step sizes, and they expect the same failure they saw when meshes varied by two orders of magnitude.

My steady RANS solver has no single solver-fidelity knob: SIMPLEC nests a pressure solve, transport solves, turbulence updates and mesh correctors with their own tolerances, convergence is non-monotone in the outer-iteration count, so the authors ran it to a fixed count and could not use the solver axis at all.

To find the optimal mixture I have to sweep lambda at my deployment budget (+170% data cost) or calibrate at three small budgets and extrapolate, which the paper admits fails on discretization axes where the optimum jumps abruptly (regret up to 99% on Poisson 2D).
